evidence: "Real 70B-class dense models commonly use grouped-query attention (GQA): LLaMA-2 70B, for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads, so per-token KV shrinks by the head ratio to KVGQA per-token = 2 × nlayers × nKV-heads × dhead × B = 2 × 80 × (8 × 128) × 2 B ≈0.33 MB/token — about 8× smaller."
issue: LLaMA-2 70B uses standard multi-head attention with 64 key/value heads (num_key_value_heads=64 = num_attention_heads), not GQA with 8 KV-heads. GQA was introduced after Llama 2's release and first used in Llama 3. The model with 8 KV-heads and the stated 0.33 MB/token arithmetic is LLaMA-3 70B, not LLaMA-2 70B. As stated, the text attributes a ~8× KV reduction to a model that would actually hold the full-MHA ~2.62 MB/token, undermining the sensitivity note's purpose of showing readers how GQA changes the KV constant.
fix_instruction: Replace "LLaMA-2 70B" with "LLaMA-3 70B" in the attention-family sensitivity note in Ch. 7 §3. Also verify that every other instance of a "Llama-2" + GQA pairing is corrected or removed (see R18-002).

evidence: "Per-request context/KV cost at 9.2K input — named 70B checkpoint with GQA‑8 (e.g. Llama‑2/3 70B)"
issue: Table 5-2 lists "Llama‑2/3 70B" as an example of a "70B checkpoint with GQA‑8." Llama-2 70B does not use GQA (it has 64 KV-heads, standard MHA). Only Llama-3 70B uses GQA with 8 KV-heads. The slash notation "2/3" naturally reads as including both generations, so readers choosing a model from this table would wrongly assume Llama-2 70B has 8× smaller KV than the full-MHA bound. This is the same attribution error as R18-001, appearing earlier in the book.
fix_instruction: Change "Llama‑2/3 70B" to "Llama‑3 70B" in Table 5-2 of Ch. 5, or to "Llama-3 70B (Llama-2 70B uses full MHA)" if the contrast is pedagogically useful.

page: PDF p. 155 (printed p. 131); also PDF p. 144 (printed p. 120) and PDF p. 146 (printed p. 122)
chapter: Ch. 6 — Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions
evidence: §6.1.1 (PDF p. 144): "Queue depth is not one of them: it is a scheduler state, a leading indicator that helps explain these serving metrics." Fig. 6.1 (PDF p. 146) carries the same box label: "queue depth: scheduler state, not a serving metric". But §6.3.4 (PDF p. 155) reads: "We see: p95 TTFT climbing (serving), KV cache hit ratio low (resource: FLOP/reuse — prefill recomputation), and prefill queue depth growing (serving)." And §6.4 (PDF p. 155): "Deploy counters at all three layers from day one — rps and token profile (workload); TTFT/TPOT/goodput percentiles and queue depth (serving — queue depth being the scheduler state that explains the others); HBM bandwidth, FLOP/MFU, KV cache occupancy, memory pressure (resource)."
issue: Queue depth is given two mutually exclusive classifications inside one chapter. §6.1.1 and Fig. 6.1 explicitly exclude it from the serving-metric layer (it is scheduler state); §6.3.4 then tags it '(serving)' in the worked dashboard trace, and §6.4 lists it inside the serving group. The metric hierarchy is the book's diagnostic spine ('never jump from a workload metric straight to a serving metric'), and §6.3.4's trace is the chapter's demonstration of reading the chain upward — so a reader following the example would place a scheduler-state counter in the serving layer, contradicting the chapter's own taxonomy and its statement that queue depth is 'a leading indicator that helps explain these serving metrics' rather than one of them.
fix_instruction: Pick one classification and apply it in all three places. Recommended: keep the §6.1.1/Fig. 6.1 taxonomy (queue depth = scheduler state, not a serving metric) and correct §6.3.4 to read 'prefill queue depth growing (scheduler state — a leading indicator of the serving symptom above)' and §6.4 to list queue depth as a separate scheduler-side counter rather than inside the serving group. If instead queue depth is to be reclassified as a serving metric, change §6.1.1 and the Fig. 6.1 box label accordingly and state the consequence for the causal chain.

evidence: §7.3.2 (PDF p. 172): "Its language configuration has 16 full-attention layers, four KV-heads per layer, and a head dimension of 256 (released configuration, retrieved 2026-10-28)." and "[1P][FACT] for the configuration, including that 262,144-token maximum context length". §7.3.3 (PDF p. 177): "[1P][FACT] for the GGUF specification content (GGUF specification, pinned revision, retrieved 2026-10-28)". By contrast the immediately preceding subsection (§7.3.1, PDF p. 171) names the revision: "These datasheets were admitted under post-cutoff addendum v20260913+addendum-20261028, outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff, as dated device-capacity documentation". The Preface (PDF p. 21) states the rule: "the separately dated 2026-10-28 technology notes in the body and Appendix A carry revision v20260913+addendum-20261028". Ch. 5's footnotes (PDF pp. 127, 139) use the partial form "retrieved 2026-10-28 (post-cutoff addendum: outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff...)" with no revision identifier.
issue: Two body subsections import post-cutoff evidence (retrieved 2026-10-28) and label it [1P][FACT] without carrying the addendum revision the Preface mandates for dated 2026-10-28 technology notes, while the sibling subsection one page earlier and the comparable Ch. 2/Ch. 3 passages do carry 'v20260913+addendum-20261028'. The Ch. 5 footnotes use a third, unnumbered form ('post-cutoff addendum:') that also fails to name the revision. Since the book's edition rule ties a revision identifier to each dated post-cutoff claim so a reader can tell which claims sit outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot, the unnamed revisions in §7.3.2/§7.3.3 break that traceability for the two claims the book treats as first-party facts (the Qwen3.8-27B attention configuration and the GGUF specification content).
fix_instruction: Add the revision identifier to every body note dated 2026-10-28: e.g. in §7.3.2 change '(released configuration, retrieved 2026-10-28)' to '(released configuration, retrieved 2026-10-28 — post-cutoff addendum v20260913+addendum-20261028, outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff)', and in §7.3.3 do the same for the GGUF specification citation. page: PDF p. 60 (printed p. 36); taxonomy at PDF p. 19–20 (printed p. xv–xvi)
chapter: Ch. 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference (§2.5 Common Mistakes)
evidence: §2.5 (PDF p. 60): "actual sustained bandwidth for weight-read kernels may be 60–80% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE: industry rule of thumb, no named survey or benchmark][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED] — not measured or cited here." The Preface (PDF p. 19) defines the Axis-1 provenance values as "[1P] — first-party: the model vendor's own spec. / [canonical scenario] — the book's own internally defined workload and model / [ILLUSTRATIVE] — a non-canonical worked-example or scenario input chosen to make a calculation concrete / [2°] — reputable second-hand / [LAB] — measured on the author's own home-lab hardware", and (PDF p. 20) states: "A label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes, e.g. [1P][DERIVED] or [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; the two tags are set with no space between them and never break across a line."
issue: The tag '[ILLUSTRATIVE: industry rule of thumb, no named survey or benchmark]' is not one of the defined Axis-1 provenance values — it embeds a free-text qualifier inside the tag, then adds a second and third axis token, producing a three-part label with an undefined first element. Everywhere else the book uses the closed vocabulary (e.g. '[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS]', '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]'), so a reader or parser following the Preface's taxonomy cannot resolve this label to a defined provenance value. The substance (an unmeasured industry rule of thumb flagged as a hypothesis) is legitimate; only the tag form is malformed.
fix_instruction: Normalize the label to the defined vocabulary: write '[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED]' and move the qualifier out of the tag into the surrounding prose (e.g. 'may be 60–80% of peak — an industry rule of thumb, with no named survey or benchmark [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED]'), matching the pattern already used elsewhere in the same chapter and in Ch. 4 §4.5.

evidence: PDF p.124 (book p.100): "the canonical 6–21-host fleet on the cloud rental basis is roughly $87.6K–$306.6K/month — the 6-host paid-occupancy $87,600 and the 21-host always-on $306,600 — (... the self-host 21-host line is a separate $155,816.93/month and lies outside this range ...)". The sidebar table (PDF p.99, book p.75) itself states the self-host line is "owned, not rented, so ~half the cloud 21-host line". 155,816.93 lies strictly inside the interval [87,600; 306,600], and its per-1K equivalent $24.97 (PDF p.99) lies inside the quoted $14.04–$49.13 per-1K range too.
issue: The relational claim "lies outside this range" is arithmetically false under every reading: the self-host monthly total $155,816.93 is contained within the quoted cloud-rental range $87.6K–$306.6K, and its per-1K figure $24.97 is contained within $14.04–$49.13. The intended meaning ("is a separate cost basis, not a point in the cloud-rental series") is contradicted by the numbers as written, and it reverses the reader's check against the sidebar's "about half" comparison.
fix_instruction: Replace "lies outside this range" with wording that names the category, not the interval, e.g. "is a separate capex+energy cost basis, not a point in this cloud-rental series" or "does not belong to the cloud-rental comparison above". Verify no other occurrence uses 'outside the range' for a value that numerically falls inside it.

evidence: Page 29, Table 2-2, row 'Prefill: single-H100 capacity': '1.29 PFLOP / ~1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS demand > 0.989 PFLOPS H100 peak; with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS...'
issue:
Arithmetic Error in Derived Value. The text states that including the attention term results in a demand of '~1.40 PFLOPS'. However, using the stated total FLOPs (~1.51 PFLOP) and the stated time (~1.08 s), the calculation is 1.51 / 1.08 ≈ 1.398, which rounds to ~1.40. Wait, re-reading the previous section (page 31, Table 2-2 scope note) and the text on page 29: 'with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS'. Let's check the linear-only demand: 1.29 / 1.08 = 1.194 -> 1.19. The text claims 1.51 PFLOPs results in 1.40 PFLOPS. 1.51 / 1.08 = 1.398. This is technically correct rounding. However, earlier in §2.3.1 (Table 2-2), the row says 'Prefill: FLOPs, linear term only... 1.29 PFLOP... excludes... attention term, which adds ~0.22 PFLOP (+17%)... -> ~1.51 PFLOP total'. 1.29 + 0.22 = 1.51. 1.51/1.08 = 1.398. The text says 1.40. This is correct. 

Let's look at another spot. Page 56, Figure 2.2 caption: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. Ridge = Peak FLOPS / Peak Bandwidth. 989 TFLOPS = 989 * 10^12 FLOP/s. 3.35 TB/s = 3.35 * 10^12 Byte/s. 989 / 3.35 ≈ 295.22. This is correct.
fix_instruction: No defect found in this specific check. The arithmetic in Table 2-2 and Fig 2.2 is consistent.
